# Introduction

The dominating method for fitting regularized regression models is proximal
coordinate descent, which serves as the default optimization method in a range
of software packages, including glmnet\ [@friedman2010; @tay2023],
biglasso\ [@zeng2017], ncvreg\ [@breheny2011], skglm\ [@bertrand2022],
adelie\ [@yang2024], LIBLINEAR\ [@fan2008; @yuan2012], and
BlitzL1\ [@johnson2015]. These packages do not in fact run a single algorithm:
glmnet, biglasso, adelie, and ncvreg solve a sequence of weighted-least-squares
subproblems via inner CD (the IRLS-CD family); LIBLINEAR and BlitzL1 do the same
with a proximal-Newton linearization\ [@lee2014]; skglm runs CD directly on the
original GLM loss with constant per-coordinate Lipschitz steps. Coordinate
descent has been investigated extensively, for instance with respect to
acceleration and parallelization, yet one aspect that has so far not been
investigated is the strategy of fitting the intercept.

In this paper, we are interested in the following optimization problem:
$$
\minimize_{\beta_0 \in \mathbb{R},\beta \in \mathbb{R}^p}
  \Big(
  P(\beta_0,\beta)
  = F(\beta_0, \beta) + G_{\lambda}(\beta)
  \Big)
$$ {#eq-primal-problem}
where $P$ is the primal objective, $F$ is the loss function, which attempts to
optimize the fit to the data, and $G$ is the penalty function that penalizes
solutions with large coefficients. $\beta_j$ is the $j$th coefficient and
$\beta_0$ is the intercept. Throughout the paper, we assume that $P$ is
separable and that $F$ is of the form
$$
F(\beta_0, \beta) = \sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i^\intercal \beta + \beta_0; y_i),
$$
where $f$ is a smooth, twice differentiable, and convex function. For brevity,
we use the convention of denoting the $i$th row and $j$th column of the design
matrix $X$ as $x_i$ and $x_j$ respectively. Finally, we let $(\hat{\beta}\_0,
\hat{\beta})$ denote a solution to the problem in @eq-primal-problem. Although
we will not generally assume that $P$ is convex, we will focus on this case in
our empirical work.

Intercepts are necessary when fitting regularized regression models, since the
results will otherwise depend on the locations (means) of both the response
vector, $y$, and the design matrix, $X$. Only under strong assumptions can the
intercept be omitted without leading to unwanted results.

Despite the importance of the intercept and the maturity of coordinate descent
as a method for fitting regularized regression models, the issue of how to
update the intercept has not been studied in the literature. This may also serve
to explain why existing CD implementations differ widely in their treatment of
it: glmnet (`type.logistic`) and biglasso (`alg.logistic`) expose a
user-selectable toggle between a local-Newton and an MM ($1/4$-Lipschitz) IRLS
surrogate, and this choice happens to also determine which intercept update is
realized---the local-Newton surrogate induces an exact 1-D Newton step on the
intercept, while the MM surrogate reduces to a constant-Lipschitz gradient
step; skglm picks the gradient scheme implicitly through its
constant-Lipschitz design; adelie keeps the intercept implicit through a weighted-centered-features
parameterization of the inner Gaussian surrogate; LIBLINEAR and BlitzL1 graft a
separate 1-D Newton convergence loop on the intercept onto each prox-Newton
subproblem. But as we show in this paper, the choice of strategy can have a
significant impact on convergence speed, especially under response imbalance.

The three main strategies that we will consider in this paper are:

Gradient Strategy
:   The intercept is updated using a single gradient step before each pass over
    the coordinates.

Newton Strategy
:   The intercept is updated using a single Newton step before each pass over
    the coordinates. We also study a *damped* version that wraps the Newton step
    in an Armijo backtracking line search; the damped variant reduces to the
    bare Newton update whenever the full step is accepted (the common case) and
    provides a safeguard in the cold-start or saturated-loss regime where bare
    Newton can overshoot.

Convergence Strategy
:   The intercept is updated by solving the optimization problem in the
    intercept convergence before each pass over the coordinates, using either
    gradient or Newton steps.

For a first illustration, see @fig-first-example, which compares the three
strategies on $\ell_1$-regularized logistic regression on the w1a dataset. The
Newton strategy reaches the optimal solution quickly, and the gradient strategy
more slowly. The convergence strategy does not make progress on this problem
under cyclic coordinate ordering --- a sensitivity we return to in
@sec-ordering.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-first-example
#| fig-cap: Overall convergence for $\ell_1$-regularized logistic regression on
#|   the real dataset w1a.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "first-example.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals])

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-20)

spec = data(df) * mapping(:time, :relgaps, color = :strategy)

layers = visual(Lines)

draw(
    layers * spec,
    axis = (; yscale = log10, ylabel = "Relative duality gap", xlabel = "Time (s)"),
    figure = (; size = (500, 300))
)
```

@fig-first-example previews the main message of this paper: the Newton strategy
is both reliable and efficient, the gradient strategy is too slow, and the
convergence strategy pays a per-pass cost without a commensurate rate gain. An
Armijo-safeguarded *damped* Newton variant protects against the narrow
cold-start regime where a bare Newton step can overshoot.

The framework we develop is both diagnostic and explanatory: it predicts when a
solver's intercept update will slow under imbalance, and it explains why most
CD-based GLM solvers in current use have already made the right structural
choice within their algorithmic family. The outliers---skglm, glmnet's
`modified.Newton` mode, biglasso's opt-in MM mode---are exactly
the cases the framework, correctly, flags as suboptimal. We see this as an
explanatory contribution about an existing design space rather than a critique
of implementations.

Our main contributions are as follows:

Strategy Taxonomy
:   We introduce and formalize three intercept-update strategies---gradient,
    Newton, and convergence---that span the design space used by current CD
    solvers for regularized GLMs, together with an Armijo-backtracking safeguard
    on the Newton strategy (the *damped Newton* variant) for the cold-start
    regime.

A Unifying Schur-Complement Analysis
:   We develop a single Schur-complement lens that parameterises each strategy
    by the cross-Hessian coupling $\rho_{0j}^2$ and the curvature ratio
    $H_{00}/L_0$. Short Taylor expansions and an envelope-theorem identity tie
    the gradient strategy's slow regime to the per-coordinate Lipschitz mismatch
    $H_{00} \ll L_0$, and a decomposition of the standard randomized-CD bound by
    coordinate yields the leading-order iteration-complexity ratio
    $T_{\mathrm{G}}/T_{\mathrm{N}} \sim L_0/H_{00}$ in the imbalance regime,
    which diverges as $\mu_0 \to 1$ for binary logistic regression.

Structural Classification of Production Solvers
:   We derive a classification of CD-based GLM solvers into four algorithmic
    families---direct CD, local-IRLS, MM-IRLS, and prox-Newton---and identify
    the intercept strategy realized by each. The classification correctly orders
    every package in our survey (glmnet, biglasso, skglm, adelie, LIBLINEAR,
    BlitzL1, ncvreg, Lasso.jl), corrects two misclassifications in the prior
    framing of LIBLINEAR and BlitzL1, and turns the within-package mode toggles
    in glmnet (`type.logistic`) and biglasso (`alg.logistic`) into a controlled
    empirical experiment.

Empirical Verification on Production Codebases
:   Five figures on the same imbalanced logistic problem confirm the framework's
    predictions: glmnet `modified.Newton` needs roughly six times more inner
    passes than `Newton`; biglasso `MM` needs roughly ten times more than
    `Newton`; skglm exhibits the predicted slow ramp; LIBLINEAR and BlitzL1 both
    converge fast, as the framework predicts for their prox-Newton +
    convergence-strategy intercept design; adelie matches the per-iteration cost
    of glmnet `Newton`, as the framework predicts for its centered-features
    local-IRLS realization.

Multinomial Extension
:   We extend the analysis to vector intercepts (multinomial logistic) and show
    that the rare-class regime turns the slowdown from a corner case into the
    common regime.

## Related Work

The intercept-update question sits at the intersection of three literatures,
none of which has analysed it as a separate quantity.

Intercept handling in CD-based GLM solvers has been treated as a routine
implementation choice across the production-CD ecosystem. The original glmnet
paper\ [@friedman2010] and its all-GLM extension\ [@tay2023] expose two weight
schemes for the logistic IRLS inner solve---local weights and a global 1/4
upper bound, surfaced as the R-package modes `type.logistic = "Newton"` and
`"modified.Newton"`---which the glmnet documentation describes as a speed
trade-off ("an upper-bound on the Hessian... can be faster") rather than as an
intercept-strategy choice. LIBLINEAR's newGLMNET solver
[@fan2008; @yuan2012] runs a 1-D Newton convergence loop on the intercept after
each prox-Newton subproblem, described in passing as an implementation detail
rather than as a design decision. The Hastie--Tibshirani--Wainwright
textbook\ [@hastie2015] keeps the intercept unpenalized but does not separate it
algorithmically from the slopes, and celer\ [@massias2020] does not support
intercepts for $\ell_1$-logistic regression. The *implementation*-side choice is
widely made and widely varied; the *analysis*-side question---under what
response distributions the choice matters---has not been posed.

A second thread is the fixed-effects tradition. For linear regression the
intercept can be partialled out: centering the features zeros the cross-Hessian
$H_{0j}$ and yields $\hat\beta_0 = \bar y$ at the unregularized optimum, leaving
the slope subproblem decoupled from the intercept. This is the Frisch--Waugh--
Lovell theorem\ [@lovell1963], and it is the argument that justifies leaving the
intercept unpenalized along the Gaussian path of glmnet. The decoupling fails
for non-Gaussian GLMs because the inverse link sits between $\beta_0$ and $y$:
the cross-Hessian acquires weights $w_i = f''(\eta_i; y_i)$ that no longer cancel
under feature centering alone, and the closed form for $\hat\beta_0$ vanishes.
adelie\ [@yang2024] supplies the natural GLM analogue: its proximal
quasi-Newton method builds a weighted Gaussian surrogate at each linearization
and absorbs the intercept implicitly through that surrogate, rather than as a
separate CD coordinate. The same argument explains why
the framework of @sec-theory has no bite on Gaussian data: there the decoupling
is already complete, $L_0 = H_{00}$, and the gradient and Newton strategies
coincide on the intercept.

The third thread is majorization--minimization. The constant $L_0 = n/4$ that
governs the gradient strategy in @lem-gradient-partial, and which skglm uses as
its global per-coordinate Lipschitz step, is the binary specialization of the
quadratic Hessian majorant used by @bohning1992 to build an MM algorithm for
multinomial logistic regression. @hunter2004 give the canonical exposition of
MM. @krishnapuram2005 apply Böhning's bound to L1-penalized multinomial logistic
regression, a direct precedent for the multinomial extension of this paper. In
regularized logistic regression the same construction lives on as the
`modified.Newton` mode of glmnet and the `MM` mode of biglasso\
(@tbl-classification). @lem-gradient-partial gives the quantitative cost: when
the response is imbalanced, $H_{00}/L_0$ shrinks to zero and the MM step loses
progress in proportion. The MM literature treats this as loose majorization;
what this paper adds is that for imbalanced logistic regression and rare-class
multinomial classification it is the common regime, not a corner case
(@sec-irls, @fig-multinomial-sweep).

## Theory {#sec-theory}

In this work, we consider models where the loss function is of the form
$$
F(\beta_0, \beta) = \sum_{i=1}^n f(x_i^\intercal \beta + \beta_0; y_i),
$$
which includes the full family of generalized linear models (GLMs). We let
$\eta : \mathbb{R} \mapsto \mathbb{R}$ be the function that maps the linear
predictor to the domain of the response variable. For GLMs, this corresponds to
the inverse link function. To simplify notation, we equivalently define $\eta\_i
= x_i^\intercal \beta + \beta\_0$ to be the linear predictor. In a GLM, the
response $y_i$ is modelled as a random variable from an exponential family, and
is assumed to depend conditionally on the linear predictor $\eta_i$ via $\E(y_i
\mid \eta\_i) = \ilink(\eta\_i)$, where $\ilink$ is the inverse link function.

To estimate the parameters of the model, $(\beta_0, \beta)$, we form a loss
function from the negative log-likelihood of the target distribution, modeling
its mean parameter through the inverse link function applied to the linear
predictor. A special property of the resulting loss function is that its partial
derivative with respect to $\eta$ is
$$
f'(\eta_i; y) = \ilink(\eta_i) - y_i = r_i,
$$
where we define $r_i$ to be the $i$th component of the *generalized residual*.
As a consequence, the gradient of the loss function with respect to $\beta_j$
can be expressed as
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_j} F(\beta_0,\beta)
  = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij} \frac{\partial}{\partial \eta_i} f(\eta_i; y_i)
  = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij} r_i.
$$

We summarize the loss, link, and inverse link functions for the loss functions
we will consider in this paper in @tbl-glm.

  | Model       | $f(\eta; y)$                                                                                       | $\link(\mu)$                           | $\ilink(\eta)$                                       |
  | :---------- | :------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | :------------------------------------- | :--------------------------------------------------- |
  | Gaussian    | $\frac{1}{2}(y - \eta)^2$                                                                          | $\mu$                                  | $\eta$                                               |
  | Binomial    | $\log(1 + e^\eta) - \eta y$                                                                        | $\log\left(\frac{\mu}{1 - \mu}\right)$ | $\frac{e^\eta}{1 + e^\eta}$                          |
  | Poisson     | $e^\eta - \eta y$                                                                                  | $\log(\mu)$                            | $e^\eta$                                             |
  | Multinomial | $\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}\left( \log \left( 1 +  \sum_{j=1}^{m-1} e^{\eta_j}\right) - y_k \eta_k  \right)$ | $\log\left(\frac{\mu}{1 - \mu}\right)$ | $\frac{\exp(\eta)}{1 + \sum_{j=1}^{m-1} e^{\eta_j}}$ |

  : Loss functions, link functions, and inverse link functions for generalized
    linear models. Note that in the case of multinomial logistic regression, the
    input is vector-valued, and we allow $\log$ and $\exp$ to be overloaded to
    apply element-wise in these cases. {#tbl-glm}

### Coordinate Descent

Coordinate descent is an iterative optimization method that updates one
coordinate at a time, while keeping the other coordinates fixed. In the case of
the intercept, this means that we update $\beta_0$ while keeping $\beta$ fixed.
In other words, we take the derivative with respect to the $j$th coefficient.
Using the chain rule, this can be expressed as
$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_j} F(\beta_0, \beta) = \sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij} f'(\eta_i; y_i)
$$

In our algorithm, we take a step in the negative gradient direction, updating a
coefficient or intercept by
$$
\beta_j^+ = \beta_j - \gamma_j \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_j} F(\beta_0, \beta),
$$
where $\gamma_j$ is the step size. The step size can be chosen in different
ways, but the typical approach in a coordinate descent algorithms is to take a
Newton step. We first compute the second derivative with respect to $\beta_j$:
$$
H_{jj} = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \beta_j^2} F(\beta_0, \beta) = \sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij}^2 f''(\eta_i; y_i),
$$

Letting $w_i = f''(\eta_i; y_i)$ be the *weights*, we can express the Hessian
diagonal element as
$$
H_{jj} = \sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij}^2 w_i.
$$

This leads to the following choice of step size:
$$
\gamma_j = H_{jj}^{-1} = \left( \sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij}^2 w_i \right)^{-1}.
$$

It may seem natural to also take a Newton step for the intercept, i.e. pick
$$
\gamma_0
= H_{00}^{-1}
= \left( \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \beta_0^2} F(\beta_0, \beta) \right)^{-1}
= \left( \sum_{i=1}^n f''(\eta_i; y_i) \right)^{-1}.
$$
But as we have already discussed, several state-of-the-art implementations of
coordinate descent for regularized regression take different approaches to
updating the intercept. The three main strategies that we have identified are
these:

1. A Newton step, setting $\gamma_0$ as above.
2. A gradient descent step, setting $\gamma_0$ to either the global Lipschitz
   constant with respect to $\beta_0$ or via a backtracking line search.
3. Solving the optimization problem of the intercept iteratively to convergence,
   using either Newton or gradient steps. In this paper, we will use Newton
   steps. And we will refer to this method as the *convergence strategy*.

The coordinate descent algorithm, with the difference intercept update
strategies, is summarized in @algo-cd.

```pseudocode
#| label: algo-cd
#| html-comment-delimiter: "//"
#| html-line-number: true
#| html-no-end: false
#| pdf-placement: "ht"
#| pdf-line-number: true

\begin{algorithm}
    \caption{Cyclic Coordinate Desccent}
    \begin{algorithmic}
        \State \textbf{Input:} Data $(X, y)$, $\lambda > 0$, initial intercept and coefficients $(\beta_0, \beta)$
        \While{not converged}
            \For{$j$ in $\{1, 2, ..., p\}$}
                \State $\beta_j \gets \operatorname{prox}\left( \beta_j - \gamma_j \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_j} F(\beta_0, \beta) \right)$
            \EndFor

            \If{intercept strategy is "Newton"}
                \State $\beta_0 \gets \beta_0 - \left( \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \beta_0^2} F(\beta_0, \beta) \right)^{-1} \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0} F(\beta_0, \beta)$
            \ElsIf{intercept strategy is "Gradient"}
                \State $\beta_0 \gets \beta_0 - \frac{1}{L_0} \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0} F(\beta_0, \beta)$
            \ElsIf{intercept strategy is "Convergence"}
                \While{not converged}
                    \State $\beta_0 \gets \beta_0 - \left( \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \beta_0^2} F(\beta_0, \beta) \right)^{-1} \frac{\partial}{\partial \beta_0} F(\beta_0, \beta)$
                \EndWhile
            \EndIf
        \EndWhile
        \State \textbf{Output:} $(\beta_0, \beta)$
    \end{algorithmic}
\end{algorithm}
```

The Newton branch of @algo-cd is the bare Newton step; the damped Newton variant
simply wraps the same direction in an Armijo backtracking line search, and we
develop it in @sec-irls.

### Cross-Influence of Intercept and Coefficients

The Hessian of $F$ with respect to the intercept and the coefficients exposes
how the intercept couples to each coefficient. Letting $w_i = f''(\eta_i; y_i)$,
we have
$$
H_{jk} = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \beta_j \partial \beta_k} F(\beta_0, \beta)
       = \sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij} x_{ik} w_i
$$
for the coefficient--coefficient block and
$$
H_{0j} = \frac{\partial^2}{\partial \beta_0 \partial \beta_j} F(\beta_0, \beta)
       = \sum_{i=1}^n x_{ij} w_i
$$
for the cross-influence between the intercept and the $j$th coefficient. Two
qualitative observations follow. First, the coefficients couple to each other
*pairwise*, through the weighted covariance structure of the features:
correlated features produce large $|H_{jk}|$, which is the classical reason
coordinate descent struggles on such designs. Second, the intercept couples to
each coefficient *globally*, through the weighted mean of that feature, with no
dependence on correlations.

For the special case of squared loss, $w_i = 1$ and $H_{0j} = \sum_i x_{ij}$, so
centering the features makes $H_{0j} = 0$ and the intercept decouples from the
coefficients entirely. For other losses the weights depend on the linear
predictor and the response, so $H_{0j}$ is a $w_i$-weighted mean of $x_{ij}$,
which is generally non-zero even after centering.

#### A Normalized Measure of Intercept--Coefficient Coupling

To quantify how strongly the intercept and the $j$th coefficient are coupled,
the natural quantity is the normalized cross-curvature
$$
\rho_{0j} \;=\; \frac{H_{0j}}{\sqrt{H_{00} H_{jj}}} \;\in\; [-1, 1],
$$ {#eq-rho}
which is invariant to rescaling of the features and the loss function, and which
the Cauchy--Schwarz inequality bounds in $[-1,1]$. The two extremes are easy to
interpret: $\rho_{0j} = 0$ means the intercept and $\beta_j$ can be optimized
independently; $|\rho_{0j}| \to 1$ means a change in $\beta_0$ is fully absorbed
by an opposite change in $\beta_j$ (or vice versa), and the two coordinates are
degenerate up to that direction.

#### The Profiled Objective

The cleanest way to see why $\rho_{0j}$ controls the impact of the intercept
update strategy is to consider the *profiled* objective obtained by optimizing
the intercept out:
$$
\tilde F(\beta) \;=\; \min_{\beta_0} F(\beta_0, \beta).
$$
A direct calculation (the Schur complement of $H_{00}$ in the full Hessian)
gives
$$
\tilde H_{jk} \;=\; H_{jk} - \frac{H_{j0} H_{0k}}{H_{00}},
$$ {#eq-schur}
and in particular
$$
\tilde H_{jj} \;=\; H_{jj}\bigl(1 - \rho_{0j}^2\bigr).
$$ {#eq-schur-diag}

@eq-schur-diag is the key relation. When $|\rho_{0j}|$ is close to $1$, the
profiled curvature $\tilde H_{jj}$ is much smaller than $H_{jj}$: most of the
diagonal curvature seen in $H$ is "borrowed" through the intercept and is
removed once the intercept is profiled out. Coordinate descent that re-optimizes
the intercept after every pass is effectively running on $\tilde F$, with
curvature $\tilde H_{jj}$; coordinate descent that leaves the intercept stale is
running on $F$, with the inflated curvature $H_{jj}$. The gap between these two
regimes is governed entirely by $\rho_{0j}^2$.

#### Strategies as Schur Approximations

This perspective lets us classify the three intercept update strategies by how
completely they remove the intercept--coefficient coupling. The key object is
the *gradient response* of the coefficient subproblem to an intercept step: if
we step $\beta_0 \mapsto \beta_0 - \alpha\,\partial_0 F$, the partial derivative
with respect to $\beta_j$ that the next coefficient update sees satisfies, to
first order in $\alpha$,
$$
\partial_j F(\beta_0 - \alpha\,\partial_0 F, \beta)
  \;=\;
  \partial_j F(\beta_0, \beta)
  - \alpha\, H_{j0}\, \partial_0 F(\beta_0, \beta).
$$ {#eq-gradient-response}
The Schur-corrected gradient $\partial_j F - (H_{j0}/H_{00})\,\partial_0 F$ is
the gradient of the profiled objective $\tilde F$ at the current $\beta$. The
three strategies differ in how closely the residual gradient in
@eq-gradient-response approximates that target.

We make this precise in three statements. The first is the substantive one and
is what justifies the profiled-objective viewpoint operationally.

::: {.theorem #thm-profile-equiv}
**(First-update profile equivalence.)** Let $F$ be twice continuously
differentiable and strictly convex in $\beta_0$ for every $\beta$, and let
$\tilde F(\beta) = \min_{\beta_0} F(\beta_0, \beta)$. Suppose the convergence
strategy has driven $\beta_0$ to the conditional minimizer
$\beta_0^{(t)} = \arg\min_{\beta_0} F(\beta_0, \beta^{(t)})$. Then the *first*
coefficient update of the next pass uses the gradient
$\partial_j F(\beta_0^{(t)}, \beta^{(t)}) = \partial_j \tilde F(\beta^{(t)})$,
and is therefore identical to a CD step on $\tilde F$ at $\beta^{(t)}$ with step
size $1/H_{jj}$. The step size satisfies $1/H_{jj} \leq 1/\tilde H_{jj}$ by
@eq-schur-diag, so it is a valid descent step size for $\tilde F$.
:::

::: {.proof}
By construction $\partial_0 F(\beta_0^{(t)}, \beta^{(t)}) = 0$. The envelope
theorem gives $\partial_j \tilde F(\beta^{(t)}) =
\partial_j F(\beta_0^{(t)}, \beta^{(t)})$, which is the gradient used for
the first coefficient update of the next pass. The Hessian relation
$\tilde H_{jj} = H_{jj}(1 - \rho_{0j}^2) \leq H_{jj}$ yields the step-size
ordering.
:::

@thm-profile-equiv is the bridge between the Schur analysis and CD theory: *at
the start of each pass*, the convergence strategy aligns with CD on $\tilde F$.
The catch is that this alignment lasts for exactly one coefficient update---by
the second update, $\beta_0^{(t)}$ is no longer the conditional minimizer, and
the equivalence breaks. The next lemma quantifies how quickly.

::: {.lemma #lem-convergence-cost}
**(Within-pass intercept drift undoes the convergence strategy's work.)**
Starting from $\beta_0^{(t)}$ with
$\partial_0 F(\beta_0^{(t)}, \beta^{(t)}) = 0$, a single coefficient update
$\beta_j^{(t)} \mapsto \beta_j^{(t)} + \delta_j$ yields
$$
\partial_0 F\bigl(\beta_0^{(t)}, \beta^{(t)} + \delta_j e_j\bigr)
  \;=\;
  H_{0j}\,\delta_j + O(\delta_j^2).
$$ {#eq-intercept-drift}
Hence after a single coordinate update of pass $t+1$, the intercept gradient is
no longer zero, and the conditional-minimizer property that @thm-profile-equiv
depends on is lost.
:::

::: {.proof}
Taylor-expand $\partial_0 F$ in the $\beta_j$ direction around
$(\beta_0^{(t)}, \beta^{(t)})$ using $\partial_{0j} F = H_{0j}$ and
$\partial_0 F(\beta_0^{(t)}, \beta^{(t)}) = 0$.
:::

The practical reading of @lem-convergence-cost is a *cost-versus-progress*
verdict on the convergence strategy. Let $k_0$ denote the number of inner Newton
steps consumed at the end of a pass to drive $|\partial_0 F| < \varepsilon$.
Because the intercept subproblem $\beta_0 \mapsto F(\beta_0, \beta)$ is a smooth
strongly convex 1D problem ($\partial_{00} F = H_{00} > 0$ in a neighbourhood of
its minimizer), Newton on it converges quadratically and
$k_0 = O(\log\log(1/\varepsilon))$---a small constant in practice. The empirical
decomposition in @fig-per-pass-cost confirms $k_0 \in [1, 6]$ across the
imbalance sweep. Each step costs $O(n)$ work. By the lemma, the
conditional-optimum status established by these $k_0$ steps survives exactly one
coefficient update of the next pass---by the second update it has drifted by
$H_{0j}\,\delta_j$. Outer progress is therefore upper-bounded by what one Newton
step on the intercept would have already delivered, since the first coefficient
update is the only one that benefits from the envelope alignment. The
convergence strategy thus pays $k_0 - 1 = O(\log\log(1/\varepsilon))$ extra
inner Newton steps per pass with no commensurate per-pass rate improvement over
the Newton strategy. The overhead is bounded, not unbounded, but the verdict
stands: every pass pays for inner work that buys no faster outer convergence.
The penalty grows with the magnitude of intercept-coefficient coupling: when
several $|H_{0j}|$ are large, fitting the intercept tightly is wasted work
because the next coordinate sweep re-perturbs $\partial_0 F$ immediately.

This same drift phenomenon also explains the empirical observation in
@fig-first-example: with cyclic ordering, the same set of strongly coupled
coordinates is visited in the same sequence each pass, and the intercept fit is
repeatedly disrupted in a coherent direction. The interaction with the post-pass
line search in cyclic CD can stall progress entirely. The Newton strategy, which
never overcommits to the conditional minimizer, sidesteps this pathology.

The cost-versus-progress verdict above is sharpest in the cold-start, direct-CD
setting that drives this paper. Three regimes soften it. *Warm-started path
solves* along a $\lambda$ grid begin each subproblem with $|\partial_0 F|$
already small, so $k_0$ drops to one or two inner Newton steps and the $k_0 - 1$
penalty shrinks to zero---bare Newton and the convergence strategy converge to
each other in this regime. *Strongly coupled designs*, where the envelope
alignment of @thm-profile-equiv buys a meaningful first-update gain, partially
offset the per-pass overhead, though the cyclic drift in @lem-convergence-cost
still applies. *At the prox-Newton or IRLS linearization boundary*, the Hessian
is recomputed for the next subproblem and the within-pass drift critique no
longer bites; we return to this case in @sec-irls, where it underwrites the
design choices of LIBLINEAR and BlitzL1. The convergence strategy is a
defensible choice in these regimes and the recommendation against it in the rest
of this paper should be read as scoped to the cold-start, direct-CD setting
outside all three.

::: {.lemma #lem-newton-approx}
**(Newton strategy is a leading-order approximation.)** Suppose $f$ is
three-times continuously differentiable. A single Newton step on the intercept
satisfies
$$
\bigl|\beta_0^{\text{Newton}} - \beta_0^*(\beta)\bigr|
  \;=\;
  O\!\left(\frac{\sup_\xi |f'''(\xi)|}{H_{00}^2}\,
            \bigl(\partial_0 F\bigr)^2\right),
$$ {#eq-newton-error}
where $\beta_0^*(\beta) = \arg\min_{\beta_0} F(\beta_0, \beta)$. For squared
loss, $f''' \equiv 0$ and the Newton step is exact.
:::

::: {.proof}
Standard one-step Newton error bound applied to the one-dimensional intercept
subproblem $\beta_0 \mapsto F(\beta_0, \beta)$ at the iterate $\beta_0$.
:::

@lem-newton-approx says that the Newton strategy matches the convergence
strategy at leading order, with an error that vanishes both as the iterates
approach the conditional optimum and as the third derivative shrinks. For
logistic regression $|f'''|$ is bounded by a small constant; for squared loss
the Newton step is exact and the two strategies coincide.

What we actually need to know is whether the Newton residual harms the *next*
coefficient update. The following corollary translates the one-step Newton error
into a perturbation of the coefficient gradient that the subsequent CD pass
sees.

::: {.corollary #cor-newton-coupling}
**(Newton residual perturbs the next coefficient gradient.)** Let $r_0 =
\beta_0^{\text{Newton}} - \beta_0^*(\beta)$ be the Newton residual, with
$|r_0|$ bounded as in @lem-newton-approx. The first coefficient update of
the next pass uses
$$
\partial_j F\bigl(\beta_0^{\text{Newton}}, \beta\bigr)
  \;=\;
  \partial_j \tilde F(\beta)
  \;+\; H_{j0}\, r_0
  \;+\; O(r_0^2),
$$ {#eq-newton-coupling}
i.e. the profiled gradient plus a bias of order $H_{j0} r_0$. The Newton
strategy is therefore as good as the convergence strategy on a coordinate
$j$ whenever
$$
|H_{j0}| \cdot |r_0| \;\ll\; \bigl|\partial_j \tilde F(\beta)\bigr|.
$$ {#eq-newton-good-enough}
:::

::: {.proof}
Taylor-expand $\partial_j F$ in $\beta_0$ around the conditional minimizer
$\beta_0^*(\beta)$, using $\partial_j F(\beta_0^*, \beta) = \partial_j
\tilde F(\beta)$ and $\partial_{0j} F = H_{j0}$.
:::

The criterion in @eq-newton-good-enough has two regimes worth flagging.
*Asymptotically*, $|r_0| = O((\partial_0 F)^2)$ shrinks quadratically while
$|\partial_j \tilde F|$ shrinks linearly with the iterate's distance from the
optimum, so the bias becomes negligible. *Far from the optimum*, the inequality
can fail when $|f'''|/H_{00}^2$ is large and $|\partial_0 F|$ is large
simultaneously: this is the cold-start regime, particularly for losses where
$f'''$ grows with $\eta$ such as Poisson ($f''' = e^\eta$). In that regime the
linear model implicit in a single Newton step becomes a poor approximation, and
a safeguard, such as backtracking the Newton step until the loss decreases,
recovers the leading-order accuracy that @cor-newton-coupling promises.

We emphasise that @lem-newton-approx and @cor-newton-coupling are *local* Taylor
statements about a single Newton step at the current iterate; we do not prove
global convergence for CD with the Newton intercept strategy, and rely on the
empirical evidence in §Numerical experiments for that question.

::: {.lemma #lem-gradient-partial}
**(Gradient strategy applies a fraction of the coupling correction.)** In
the local quadratic model of $F$ at $(\beta_0, \beta)$, the gradient
strategy with step size $\alpha = 1/L_0$ removes a fraction $H_{00}/L_0
\in (0, 1]$ of the coupling component $(H_{j0}/H_{00})\,\partial_0 F$ that
the Newton and convergence strategies remove. Specifically, the residual
gradient after the intercept step is
$$
\partial_j F^{\text{grad}}
  \;=\;
  \partial_j F
  - \frac{H_{00}}{L_0}\,\frac{H_{j0}}{H_{00}}\,\partial_0 F,
$$ {#eq-grad-residual}
so the coupling residual is $(1 - H_{00}/L_0)$ of its pre-step value. In
particular, when $L_0 = \infty$, no coupling is removed.
:::

::: {.proof}
Substitute $\alpha = 1/L_0$ into @eq-gradient-response and rearrange.
:::

The qualitative reading of @lem-gradient-partial is that the gradient strategy
is fully effective only when $H_{00} \approx L_0$, that is, when the Lipschitz
bound is tight at the current iterate. Whenever $H_{00}$ is appreciably below
$L_0$---as happens for logistic regression once predictions become confident, or
whenever the weights $w_i$ are concentrated on a small subset of
observations---the gradient strategy leaves a residual coupling of order
$(1 - H_{00}/L_0)$ uncorrected, and coordinate descent continues to run on a
worse-conditioned objective than necessary.

The Poisson loss is the limiting case: $H_{00}$ has no global upper bound, so
$L_0 = \infty$ and $H_{00}/L_0 = 0$. By @lem-gradient-partial, the gradient
strategy applies no coupling correction at all and the coefficient subproblem
sees the full, uncorrected gradient. In this regime the strategy is not merely
slow but structurally inadequate.

#### Quantitative Rate Gap

The $H_{00}/L_0$ ratio also enters standard randomized-CD rate bounds, where it
controls how aggressively the gradient strategy can update the intercept.
Standard sublinear bounds for randomized proximal CD
[@wright2015; @nesterov2012; @richtarik2014] grow with a sum over coordinates of
a quantity of the form $L_j R_j^2$, where $L_j$ is the coordinate-wise Lipschitz
constant and $R_j$ the cold-start distance to the optimum along coordinate $j$.
The strategies enter this expression identically on coefficient coordinates but
differently on the intercept: the gradient strategy plugs in the global
$L_0 = n\sup f''$, while the Newton and convergence strategies use the
iterate-level $H_{00}$, which may be orders of magnitude smaller.

::: {.corollary #cor-rate-gap}
**(Rate gap, leading order in imbalance.)** Let
$R_j^2 = (\beta_j^{(0)} - \beta_j^\star)^2$ denote the squared cold-start
distance to the optimum along coordinate $j$, with the intercept as coordinate
$0$. Decomposing the standard sublinear randomized-CD bound by coordinate yields
the iteration-complexity ratio
$$
\frac{T_{\mathrm{G}}(\varepsilon)}{T_{\mathrm{N}}(\varepsilon)}
  \;\lesssim\;
  \frac{L_0\,R_0^2
        + \sum_{j\ge 1} H_{jj}\bigl(1 - (H_{00}/L_0)\,\rho_{0j}^2\bigr)\,R_j^2}
       {H_{00}\,R_0^2
        + \sum_{j\ge 1} H_{jj}\bigl(1 - \rho_{0j}^2\bigr)\,R_j^2}.
$$ {#eq-rate-gap}
When the optimal intercept $|\beta_0^\star|$ is large compared to
$\|\beta^\star\|$---for binary logistic regression with cold start,
$|\beta_0^\star| = |\mathrm{logit}(\mu_0)|$ diverges as $\mu_0 \to 1$---the
intercept term dominates both numerator and denominator, and the bound reduces
at leading order to
$$
\frac{T_{\mathrm{G}}(\varepsilon)}{T_{\mathrm{N}}(\varepsilon)}
  \;\sim\;
  \frac{L_0}{H_{00}(\hat\eta)}.
$$ {#eq-rate-gap-asymptotic}
For logistic regression, $L_0 = n/4$ stays fixed while $H_{00}(\hat\eta) \to 0$
as imbalance grows, so the ratio diverges.
:::

::: {.proof}
Apply the standard sublinear randomized-CD bound separately for each
strategy. The Newton strategy's intercept update is exact at leading order
(@lem-newton-approx) and aligns with CD on the profiled objective $\tilde
F$ (@thm-profile-equiv), whose coefficient curvatures are
$\tilde H_{jj} = H_{jj}(1-\rho_{0j}^2)$ by @eq-schur-diag. The gradient
strategy uses the global Lipschitz $L_0$ on the intercept and, by
@lem-gradient-partial, removes only fraction $H_{00}/L_0$ of the coupling,
leaving an effective coefficient curvature
$H_{jj}\bigl(1 - (H_{00}/L_0)\rho_{0j}^2\bigr)$. Substituting these into the
$L_j R_j^2$ sum gives @eq-rate-gap. The asymptotic reduction in
@eq-rate-gap-asymptotic follows by retaining only the $R_0^2$ term in the
$|\beta_0^\star|/\|\beta^\star\| \to \infty$ limit.
:::

Two regimes inside @eq-rate-gap are worth flagging. **Strongly coupled designs**
($\bar\rho^2 \to 1$, e.g. uncentered designs where the intercept absorbs the
column means): the denominator's Schur term collapses and the ratio gains an
additional factor of order $1/(1-\bar\rho^2)$. **Standardized designs**
($\rho_{0j} \approx 0$): the Schur correction is inactive, but
@eq-rate-gap-asymptotic still diverges via the intercept's $R_0^2$ dominance.
The two channels---per-coordinate Lipschitz mismatch on the intercept, and Schur
coupling propagated to the coefficients---are independent, and both ride on the
same $H_{00}/L_0 \to 0$ regime.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-rate-gap
#| fig-cap: Empirical $T_{\mathrm{G}}/T_{\mathrm{N}}$ (pass count to relative
#|   gap $10^{-6}$) versus the leading-order predicted ratio
#|   $L_0/H_{00}(\hat\eta)$ from @eq-rate-gap-asymptotic, swept over response
#|   imbalance $\mu_0$ on the standardized logistic problem of @fig-mu-extreme
#|   ($n = 500$, $p = 1000$, $s = 10$, $\lambda = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$). The
#|   two curves track in scaling, with the empirical multiplier a small constant
#|   below the asymptotic prediction — consistent with the prediction being a
#|   leading-order limit that incorporates only the intercept-coordinate
#|   contribution.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "rate-gap.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["records"])
df.L0_over_H00 = df.L0 ./ df.H00
df_long = stack(
    df,
    [:empirical_ratio, :L0_over_H00];
    variable_name = :quantity,
    value_name = :ratio,
)
df_long.quantity = map(df_long.quantity) do q
    q == "empirical_ratio" ? "Empirical T_G / T_N" :
    "Predicted L₀ / H₀₀"
end

spec = data(df_long) * mapping(:μ0, :ratio, color = :quantity)

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec + visual(Scatter) * spec,
    axis = (
        yscale = log10,
        xlabel = "Response imbalance μ₀",
        ylabel = "T_G / T_N",
    ),
    figure = (; size = (550, 300)),
)
```

@fig-rate-gap shows the prediction holds in scaling: as $\mu_0 \to 1$, both
empirical $T_{\mathrm{G}}/T_{\mathrm{N}}$ and the asymptotic predictor
$L_0/H_{00}(\hat\eta)$ grow together, with the empirical multiplier sitting a
small constant factor below the prediction. The prediction is leading order, so
a constant gap is expected: subdominant $\sum_j R_j^2$ terms in @eq-rate-gap
dilute the intercept's dominance, and the convergence-strategy result of
@thm-profile-equiv is not exact for cyclic CD past the first coordinate update.
The scaling, not the constant, is the load-bearing prediction.

@cor-rate-gap connects directly to §Production solvers. glmnet's
`modified.Newton` mode and biglasso's `MM` mode both apply the gradient strategy
at the global $L_0 = n/4$ to the intercept inside their IRLS inner solves; the
corollary predicts their pass counts should grow with $L_0/H_{00}$ at
$\mu_0 = 0.99$, matching the empirical ≈6× and ≈10× slowdowns reported in
@fig-real-glmnet and @fig-real-biglasso. skglm, the direct-CD solver, exhibits
the same scaling on a continuous trajectory in @fig-real-skglm: the slow ramp
from suboptimality $\sim 10^{-1}$ to $\sim 10^{-5}$ is the intercept climb to
$\mathrm{logit}(\mu_0)$ at step size $1/L_0$.

An obvious objection to @lem-gradient-partial is that adaptive step sizing
should rescue the gradient strategy: an Armijo line search ought to shrink
$\alpha$ until the iterate makes progress, irrespective of $L_0$. But starting
from the global-Lipschitz step $-\partial_0 F / L_0$ Armijo only *shrinks* the
step, and shrinking is the wrong direction when $H_{00} \ll L_0$: the step is
already too small, not too large. To recover the iterate-level curvature
$H_{00}$ a line search would need to *expand* the step beyond $1/L_0$, settling
near $1/H_{00}$. But the step of size $1/H_{00}$ applied to the gradient
direction is exactly the bare Newton step, and wrapping it in Armijo
backtracking is the damped Newton variant developed in the next subsection.
Rescuing the gradient strategy collapses it into Newton. @fig-mu-extreme
confirms the shrinking-doesn't-help direction empirically: a backtracking-Armijo
variant of the gradient strategy stalls identically to the bare-Lipschitz
version, because the Lipschitz step satisfies the sufficient-decrease condition
on the first attempt and the line search never fires.

The picture matches what production direct-CD solvers do. skglm [@bertrand2022]
uses constant per-coordinate Lipschitz steps, including $L_0 = n/4$ for the
intercept---exactly the gradient strategy as defined above, with no line search
of any kind. The other CD-based production packages we surveyed (glmnet,
biglasso, LIBLINEAR, BlitzL1) embed the intercept update inside an outer IRLS or
proximal-Newton linearization; we return to them in @sec-irls. None of the
production CD solvers we surveyed use a growth-allowing line search on the
intercept alone.

#### A Safe Newton Variant

@cor-newton-coupling identifies the cold-start regime---large $|\partial_0 F|$
combined with rapidly varying $f''$---as the setting where a bare Newton step on
the intercept perturbs the next coefficient pass enough to matter. The natural
fix is to wrap the Newton direction $-\partial_0 F / H_{00}$ in an Armijo
backtracking line search: accept the full step ($\alpha = 1$) if it decreases
$F$ enough, otherwise halve $\alpha$ until it does. We refer to this variant as
the *damped Newton strategy*. The cost is a constant number of loss evaluations
per pass in the easy regime and a logarithmic number when the linear model is
inadequate. When the Newton residual is small, $\alpha = 1$ is accepted on the
first attempt and the damped Newton strategy reduces to the Newton strategy
exactly.

#### Constructed Failure Examples

We illustrate the predictions of the strategy comparison on synthetic
logistic-regression problems with $n = 500$, $p = 1000$, $s = 10$, and
$\lambda = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-mu-extreme
#| fig-cap: As the response imbalance $\mu_0$ approaches one, the gradient
#|   strategy fails to reach the convergence tolerance within 1000 outer passes
#|   (Lemma 3.3 prediction $H_{00}/L_0 \to 0$). A backtracking-Armijo variant of
#|   the gradient strategy stalls identically---the Lipschitz step satisfies
#|   sufficient decrease on the first attempt, so the line search never shrinks
#|   $\alpha$. The Newton, damped Newton, and convergence strategies are
#|   unaffected. Randomized cyclic CD.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-mu-extreme.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals])

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-20)
df.μ0 = "μ₀ = " .* string.(df.μ0)

spec = data(df) * mapping(:time, :relgaps, color = :strategy, col = :μ0)

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10, ylabel = "Relative duality gap", xlabel = "Time (s)"),
    facet = (; linkxaxes = :none),
    figure = (; size = (800, 250))
)
```

The first prediction is @lem-gradient-partial: the gradient strategy's
correction is multiplied by $H_{00}/L_0$, which collapses as the response
imbalance $\mu_0$ approaches one. @fig-mu-extreme shows exactly this collapse:
the gradient strategy plateaus and fails to reach the tolerance within the
outer-pass budget at $\mu_0 = 0.99$, while the other strategies are essentially
unaffected.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-cold-start
#| fig-cap: With cyclic ordering and a cold-start intercept, the bare Newton
#|   strategy requires more outer passes than damped Newton at extreme
#|   imbalance. The Armijo line search of damped Newton absorbs the initial
#|   large $|\partial_0 F|$ transient that @cor-newton-coupling identifies as
#|   the failure mode of bare Newton.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-cold-start.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals])

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-20)
df.μ0 = "μ₀ = " .* string.(df.μ0)

spec = data(df) * mapping(:time, :relgaps, color = :strategy, col = :μ0)

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10, ylabel = "Relative duality gap", xlabel = "Time (s)"),
    facet = (; linkxaxes = :none),
    figure = (; size = (800, 250))
)
```

The second prediction is @cor-newton-coupling: the Newton strategy can be
perturbed by a large $|\partial_0 F|$ at cold start. @fig-cold-start exposes
this: with cyclic ordering and the intercept initialized at zero (so
$|\partial_0 F|$ is large at pass one), bare Newton needs noticeably more outer
passes than damped Newton at $\mu_0 = 0.99$. At moderate imbalance the two are
indistinguishable, consistent with @cor-newton-coupling promising leading-order
agreement whenever $|r_0|$ is small. The convergence strategy is competitive in
this experiment but pays the within-pass-drift cost identified in
@lem-convergence-cost; see also the cyclic-CD instability footnoted under
@fig-first-example.

#### Extension to vector intercepts

The scalar story extends almost verbatim to multinomial logistic regression with
$K$ classes, where the intercept is a vector $\beta_0 \in \mathbb{R}^{K-1}$
under the reference-class parameterisation $\eta_{iK} = 0$. Writing
$\eta_{ik} = x_i^\intercal \beta_k + \beta_{0k}$ for $k = 1, \dots, K-1$ and
$p_{ik} = e^{\eta_{ik}}/\bigl(1 + \sum_{l<K} e^{\eta_{il}}\bigr)$, the
per-observation Hessian block has diagonal $p_{ik}(1 - p_{ik})$ and off-diagonal
$-p_{ik} p_{il}$. The intercept Hessian
$H_{00} = \sum_i \bigl(\operatorname{diag}(p_{i,1:K-1}) - p_{i,1:K-1} p_{i,1:K-1}^\intercal\bigr)$
is a $(K-1) \times (K-1)$ matrix; the Newton strategy becomes a small block
solve $\delta = -H_{00}^{-1}\,\nabla_0 F$, and the damped variant performs
Armijo backtracking on the loss along that direction. @thm-profile-equiv,
@lem-convergence-cost, and @cor-newton-coupling all carry through with
matrix-valued $H_{00}$ in place of the scalar.

@lem-gradient-partial sharpens. The gradient strategy applies a uniform
Lipschitz bound $L_0$ across all classes, so the per-class fraction of the
correction is $H_{00,kk}/L_0 = \bigl(\sum_i p_{ik}(1 - p_{ik})\bigr)/L_0$. With
$K$ classes the diagonal $H_{00,kk}$ scales linearly with class prevalence, so
any rare class produces a microscopic intercept correction along that coordinate
while the dominant classes are well fit. Class imbalance is no longer a corner
case---with $K = 10$ and a uniform marginal, $\bar p_k = 0.1$ already, and
typical text or image-classification label distributions skew further. The
multinomial setting is where the imbalance failure of the gradient strategy is
the *common* regime rather than an extreme.

We implement block coordinate descent over classes: for each feature $j$ we
cycle through the $K-1$ class coefficients with element-wise $\ell_1$
soft-thresholding, and the intercept is updated as a vector once per pass. An
alternative is to cycle one class at a time with the others held fixed, as in
glmnet's symmetric-multinomial path; we return to that scheme below after the
block-CD findings.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-multinomial-imbalance
#| fig-cap: Imbalanced multinomial logistic ($K = 5$, marginal class
#|   probabilities $(0.7, 0.1, 0.1, 0.05, 0.05)$, $n = 500$, $p = 200$, $\lambda
#|   = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$, three random seeds, cyclic CD). The gradient
#|   strategy stalls along the rare-class intercept components, exactly as
#|   predicted by the per-class fraction-of-correction $H_{00,kk}/L_0$. The
#|   Newton, damped Newton, and convergence strategies are visually
#|   indistinguishable; the K-class block update damps the overshoot that
#|   distinguished them in the scalar setting.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-multinomial-imbalance.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals])

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-20)
df.it = "seed = " .* string.(df.it)

spec = data(df) * mapping(:time, :relgaps, color = :strategy, col = :it)

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10, ylabel = "Relative primal suboptimality", xlabel = "Time (s)"),
    facet = (; linkxaxes = :none),
    figure = (; size = (800, 250))
)
```

@fig-multinomial-imbalance reports relative primal suboptimality measured
against the lowest primal observed during each run; the multinomial CD solver
does not maintain a duality scaling. Two qualitative findings, only one of which
we predicted from the scalar theory.

The gradient strategy stalls, as expected. With the marginal class probabilities
above, the rare-class diagonal entries $H_{00,4,4}, H_{00,5,5}$ are roughly
twentieth-of-$L_0$ small, and the gradient strategy's per-class correction along
those coordinates is correspondingly microscopic. The strategy converges to the
same primal but takes roughly an order of magnitude longer.

The Newton, damped Newton, and convergence strategies collapse to a single
visible curve. This is genuinely surprising at first glance: the scalar
cold-start figure (@fig-cold-start) showed a measurable wedge between bare and
damped Newton at $\mu_0 = 0.99$, and the imbalance regime here is at least as
severe. The explanation lies in the block structure of the Newton step. In the
scalar setting, the failure mode of @cor-newton-coupling is a single-coordinate
overshoot driven by a large $|\partial_0 F|$. In the $(K-1)$-vector intercept,
the off-diagonal coupling $H_{00,kl} = -\sum_i p_{ik} p_{il}$ spreads each
per-class correction across all class intercepts jointly, so the rare-class step
is computed in concert with the dominant-class step rather than being amplified
proportionally to the rare-class gradient. The block solve provides the same
safeguarding that Armijo backtracking provides scalar-coordinate-wise.
@fig-multinomial-sweep extends the test to a 2-D grid that shrinks the rarest
class probability $\bar p_K$ down to $0.005$ and grows the feature amplitude to
four times the anchor value. The Newton-block trio collapses to a single visible
curve in every one of the sixteen cells, while the gradient strategy stalls
monotonically harder as $\bar p_K$ shrinks and as amplitude grows. This is
consistent with a structural property of the $(K-1)$-block Hessian rather than a
tuning artifact of the single anchor configuration.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-multinomial-sweep
#| fig-cap: Multinomial logistic sweep over the rarest-class marginal $\bar p_K
#|   \in \{0.05, 0.02, 0.01, 0.005\}$ (rows, top to bottom) and feature
#|   amplitude $\in \{0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0\}$ (columns, left to right), on the
#|   same $K=5$, $n=500$, $p=200$, $s=5$, $\lambda = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$,
#|   $\rho = 0.3$ design as @fig-multinomial-imbalance. Relative primal
#|   suboptimality versus outer-pass index, median over three seeds. The bare
#|   Newton, damped Newton, and convergence strategies overlap on a single curve
#|   in every cell; the gradient strategy stalls progressively harder as $\bar
#|   p_K$ shrinks (down the rows) and as amplitude grows (across the columns).
#|   The anchor cell (top-left) reproduces the trajectories of
#|   @fig-multinomial-imbalance.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-multinomial-imbalance-sweep.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals, :pass])

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-20)

agg = combine(
    groupby(df, [:p_K, :amplitude, :strategy, :pass]),
    :relgaps => median => :relgaps,
)

agg.p_K_str = "p̄_K = " .* string.(agg.p_K)
agg.amp_str = "amp = " .* string.(agg.amplitude)

spec = data(agg) * mapping(
    :pass => "Pass",
    :relgaps => "Relative primal suboptimality",
    color = :strategy,
    row = :p_K_str => sorter("p̄_K = 0.05", "p̄_K = 0.02", "p̄_K = 0.01", "p̄_K = 0.005"),
    col = :amp_str => sorter("amp = 0.5", "amp = 1.0", "amp = 1.5", "amp = 2.0"),
)

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10,),
    facet = (; linkxaxes = :none),
    figure = (; size = (800, 600)),
)
```

Practically, this simplifies the recommendation in the multinomial setting: use
the bare Newton block step. The damping safeguard that mattered for the scalar
cold-start is already built in.

The class-by-class scheme of glmnet's symmetric-multinomial path tells a
different but parallel story. Holding all $\eta_{il}$ for $l \neq k$ fixed, the
marginal subproblem in class $k$'s linear predictors $\eta_{ik}$ is, up to a
per-observation offset $\log\bigl(1 + \sum_{l \neq k} e^{\eta_{il}}\bigr)$, a
scalar logistic regression. The scalar theory of @lem-gradient-partial therefore
applies *per class*, and any rare class with extreme per-class response
imbalance triggers exactly the gradient-strategy failure documented in the
binary setting---now along the rare class's intercept coordinate specifically.
The multinomial setting hits the gradient-strategy failure mode through two
independent mechanisms then: rare-class diagonal scaling under block CD, and
rare-class scalar imbalance under class-by-class CD. The Newton-strategy
recommendation transfers to both schemes.

### Connection to IRLS {#sec-irls}

The analysis so far targets *direct* coordinate descent on $F$, in which the
weights $w_i = f''(\eta_i; y_i)$ are recomputed after every coefficient
update. A widely used alternative---and the one taken by glmnet
[@friedman2010]---is iteratively reweighted least squares (IRLS)
[@mccullagh1989]: at the current iterate $(\beta_0^{(t)}, \beta^{(t)})$,
form a weighted least squares majorizer
$$
\tilde F^{(t)}(\beta_0, \beta)
  \;=\;
  \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i=1}^n w_i^{(t)}
    \bigl( z_i^{(t)} - \beta_0 - x_i^\intercal \beta \bigr)^2,
$$
with working response $z_i^{(t)} = \eta_i^{(t)} - r_i^{(t)} / w_i^{(t)}$,
run inner CD on $\tilde F^{(t)}$, then re-linearize. Two weight choices are
used in practice: *local* weights $w_i^{(t)} = f''(\eta_i^{(t)}; y_i)$
(glmnet's `type.logistic = "Newton"`), and *MM-majorized* weights replacing
$w_i^{(t)}$ by a global upper bound on $f''$ (e.g. $w_i \equiv 1/4$ for
logistic; glmnet's `type.logistic = "modified.Newton"`, following the MM
tradition of @hunter2004).

Inside one inner solve with local weights, $\tilde F^{(t)}$ is quadratic in
$\beta_0$ with curvature $\sum_i w_i^{(t)} = H_{00}$, so the inner Lipschitz
constant satisfies $L_0^{\text{inner}} = H_{00}$. The fraction
$H_{00} / L_0^{\text{inner}} = 1$ in @lem-gradient-partial, and Newton on a
quadratic is exact, so the gradient, Newton, and convergence strategies all
coincide on the inner subproblem. The strategy distinction this paper analyzes
is therefore specific to direct-CD solvers (e.g. skglm) and does not arise
within one local-weight IRLS inner solve.

The MM-majorized variant tells a different story. Replacing $w_i^{(t)}$ by the
constant majorant $1/4$ in the logistic case, the closed-form inner intercept
update on $\tilde F^{(t)}$ is
$$
\beta_0 \;\gets\; \beta_0 + \frac{4}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - p_i)
  \;=\; \beta_0 - \frac{1}{L_0}\, \partial_0 F,
\qquad L_0 = n/4,
$$
which is exactly the gradient strategy of this paper, taken with the global
Lipschitz step. @lem-gradient-partial therefore applies directly to glmnet's
`modified.Newton` mode: under response imbalance, the per-iteration correction
fraction $H_{00} / L_0$ shrinks and the intercept update slows in proportion,
approaching a true stall only in the limit $\mu_0 \to 1$. There is a historical
irony here---MM majorization was introduced for numerical stability of the
working response $z_i$ when $w_i \to 0$, which is the same imbalance regime
where the resulting update converges slowly. For Poisson loss no global upper
bound on $f''$ exists, so the MM construction is not directly available; glmnet
uses local-weight IRLS for Poisson, where the collapse of the previous paragraph
applies instead.

Across IRLS linearizations the weights $w_i^{(t)}$ change with $\eta^{(t)}$, so
even a fully resolved inner intercept becomes stale once the weights are
recomputed. This outer-level drift is analogous to but distinct from the
within-pass drift of @lem-convergence-cost, which is direct-CD-specific.

The practical map is therefore richer than the direct-CD analysis alone
suggests. @tbl-classification summarises where each production solver falls.
Among the CD-based packages we surveyed, only skglm is a genuine
direct-CD-gradient-strategy realization on the original loss.^[We have submitted
a pull request to skglm proposing a Newton intercept update; see
<https://github.com/scikit-learn-contrib/skglm/pull/337>.] The remaining
solvers---glmnet, biglasso, adelie, LIBLINEAR, BlitzL1, Lasso.jl, ncvreg---all
linearize before doing CD, either via IRLS or via proximal-Newton on a quadratic
upper bound. Within those families the within-package mode toggles are what
isolate the strategy comparison: glmnet's `Newton` vs `modified.Newton` and
biglasso's `Newton` vs `MM` toggle precisely the weight scheme of
@lem-gradient-partial. (Scikit-learn's L1-logistic path either delegates to
LIBLINEAR or uses SAGA, the latter a variance-reduced stochastic-gradient method
that falls outside the CD framework analyzed here. celer's L1-logistic estimator
does not support an intercept at all in version 0.7.4, and its documentation
redirects users with logistic needs to skglm; it is therefore absent from the
table.)

  | Solver                                       | Family                | Intercept update on the original loss                       |
  | :------------------------------------------- | :-------------------- | :---------------------------------------------------------- |
  | skglm                                        | Constant-Lipschitz CD | Gradient ($L_0 = n/4$)                                      |
  | glmnet `type.logistic = "modified.Newton"`   | MM-IRLS               | Gradient ($L_0 = n/4$) per outer iteration                  |
  | biglasso `alg.logistic = "MM"`               | MM-IRLS               | Gradient ($L_0 = n/4$) per outer iteration                  |
  | glmnet `type.logistic = "Newton"`            | Local-IRLS            | Convergence on the local quadratic per outer iter           |
  | biglasso `alg.logistic = "Newton"` (default) | Local-IRLS            | Convergence on the local quadratic per outer iter           |
  | Lasso.jl                                     | Local-IRLS            | Convergence on the local quadratic per outer iter           |
  | ncvreg                                       | Local-IRLS            | Convergence on the local quadratic per outer iter           |
  | adelie                                       | Local-IRLS            | Implicit, via weighted-centered-features parameterization   |
  | LIBLINEAR (newGLMNET, L1-LR)                 | Prox-Newton           | Coefficient of a quadratic + post-step Newton               |
  | BlitzL1                                      | Prox-Newton           | Combined-direction backtrack + post-step Newton convergence |

  : Classification of CD-based production solvers by algorithmic family and by
    the intercept update they realize on the original loss. Local-IRLS and
    prox-Newton solvers freeze the Hessian at the start of a subproblem, so the
    three strategies of this paper coincide *within* one subproblem; the
    distinction reappears only when comparing weight schemes across outer
    iterations (rows two to five). LIBLINEAR and BlitzL1 additionally follow
    each prox-Newton subproblem with a separate sequence of 1-D Newton
    iterations on the intercept (the convergence strategy applied to the
    original loss after each outer step). {#tbl-classification}

A consequence of the table is that two production solvers---LIBLINEAR
(newGLMNET) and BlitzL1---independently chose to apply the convergence strategy
to the intercept at the boundary of each prox-Newton step. The analysis in
@lem-convergence-cost penalises convergence-strategy within direct CD because
the inner Hessian drifts between iterations; that critique does not apply at the
prox-Newton boundary, where the next subproblem's Hessian is recomputed anyway.
The structural distinction between the families thus carries over to a sensible
recommendation: use Newton on the intercept within direct CD, and run the
convergence strategy at the linearization boundary inside IRLS or prox-Newton.
The production solvers that fit serious imbalanced-GLM problems in practice
appear to have arrived at exactly this prescription.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-irls-comparison
#| fig-cap: Imbalanced logistic ($\mu_0 = 0.99$, $n = 500$, $p = 1000$, $s =
#|   10$, $\lambda = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$, three random seeds). MM-IRLS tracks
#|   Direct-CD with the gradient strategy as the algebra above predicts---both
#|   stall at the same per-iteration correction fraction. Local-weight IRLS
#|   converges, matching the strategy collapse argument. The Local-IRLS curve
#|   uses Newton at the inner level; the gradient and convergence strategies
#|   coincide with it numerically (verified in unit tests).

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-irls-comparison.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals])

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-20)
df.it = "seed = " .* string.(df.it)

spec = data(df) * mapping(:time, :relgaps, color = :strategy, col = :it)

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10, ylabel = "Relative duality gap", xlabel = "Time (s)"),
    facet = (; linkxaxes = :none),
    figure = (; size = (800, 250))
)
```

@fig-irls-comparison realizes both predictions empirically: MM-IRLS stalls on
the same plateau as Direct-CD with the gradient strategy under $\mu_0 = 0.99$,
while Local-IRLS converges on the same problem. The strategy-collapse claim
within Local-IRLS is verified numerically in the unit tests rather than the
figure, since by construction the three strategies produce identical iterates on
the inner quadratic.

A reader may notice that Local-IRLS also outpaces Direct-CD with the Newton
strategy on this problem. This reflects the broader trade-off between
algorithmic families rather than a comparison of intercept strategies: IRLS-CD
enjoys a constant inner Hessian and locally quadratic outer convergence, which
favours it on canonical-link GLMs where the linearization is tight. Direct-CD
has the edge when $f'''$ is large (e.g.\
Poisson with extreme rates, where each linearization is loose far from the
current iterate), when working-response instability under saturation matters, or
when screening and working-set methods (standard in modern $\ell_1$ solvers)
compose poorly with re-linearization [@bertrand2022]. Our strategy analysis is
orthogonal to this family choice: within either family, the recommendation
against the gradient strategy and in favour of (damped) Newton carries through.

### Geometric Illustration

```{julia}
#| label: fig-parametric
#| fig-cap: Example illustrating the three main intercept fitting strategies
#|   considered in our paper on a simple problem with one feature and an
#|   intercept.
#| fig-show: true
#| message: false

using Intercepts

n = 100
p = 1
k = 10
μ0 = 0.9

X, y = generatedata(
    n, p; response = :binomial, μ0 = μ0, x_type = :normal, x_density = 0.9, ρ = 0.99, s = k, amplitude = 1,
)

strategies = [
    (strategy = GradientStrategy(), name = "Gradient"),
    (strategy = NewtonStrategy(), name = "Newton"),
    (strategy = ConvergenceStrategy(), name = "Convergence"),
]

reg = 0.2

results = [
    cdsolver(
            X,
            y,
            reg,
            lossfun = LogisticLoss(),
            intercept_strategy = s.strategy,
            save_history = true,
        ) for s in strategies
]

λ = results[1].λ

β0 = range(-0.5, 3.5, length = 100)
β = range(-0.5, 1.2, length = 100)
grid = [(b0, b) for b0 in β0, b in β]

primal_values = zeros(size(grid))

for (i, (b0, b)) in enumerate(grid)
    η = b0 .+ X[:, 1] * b
    primal_values[i] = loss(LogisticLoss(), η, y) + λ * abs(b)
end

fig = Figure()
ax = Axis(
    fig[1, 1],
    xlabel = "Intercept (β₀)",
    ylabel = "Coefficient (β₁)",
)

levels = geomspace(minimum(primal_values), maximum(primal_values), 20)

contour!(β0, β, primal_values, levels = levels, colormap = :grays)

for (res, s) in zip(results, strategies)
    scatterlines!(res.intercepts, dropdims(res.coefs, dims = 1), label = s.name)
end

fig[1, 2] = Legend(fig, ax)

fig
```

## Results

### Methodology and Reproducibility {#sec-methodology}

All internal-solver experiments use the `Intercepts` Julia package on Julia
1.11+ with the default OpenBLAS. We report outer-pass counts as the primary work
metric: one pass is one sweep through all $p$ coordinates plus an intercept
update, and "passes to tolerance" use a target relative duality gap of $10^{-8}$
unless noted. Pass budgets (`maxit`) are set generously (1000 for the
single-$\lambda$ figures, 5000 for the heatmap of @sec-imbalance-reg) and are
clipped only at the figure level when the gradient strategy fails to reach the
tolerance; those points appear at the budget cap. All synthetic designs are
standardized (zero mean, unit variance per column) and use cyclic coordinate
ordering unless we explicitly compare orderings; the AR(1) feature correlation
parameter is $\rho = 0.6$ by default. Random seeds are fixed per experiment
script. The heatmap of @sec-imbalance-reg replicates each cell across three
seeds; the other figures use a single seed because cell-to-cell variability is
dwarfed by the strategy effect we are isolating.

Real-data experiments load LIBSVM problems via `LIBSVMdata.jl` 0.1.4 and the
solver standardizes each column internally before fitting. The production-solver
panel runs glmnet 4.1-10, biglasso 1.6-1, adelie 1.0-8, skglm 0.5, LIBLINEAR
(Python bindings of liblinear), and BlitzL1 on the shared standardized problem
produced by `experiments/sim-real-problem.jl`. Each driver sweeps its
convergence tolerance and writes a CSV under `results/real-solvers/`, which the
figures in @sec-production-solvers read directly.

All experiment outputs are cached. Internal-solver scripts at
`experiments/sim-*.jl` write `.jld2` files to `results/`; production-solver
scripts write `.csv` to `results/real-solvers/`. The paper re-renders from
cache, so to refresh a cell re-run the corresponding script. Hardware: a single
x86_64 workstation; wall-clock numbers in this paper are indicative rather than
benchmark-grade. Source code and cached results ship with the paper repository.

### Simulated Data

The first prediction we test in §Theory is @lem-gradient-partial: the gradient
strategy's effective per-pass step on the intercept is the bare gradient step
shrunk by $H_{00}/L_0$, so the strategy slows as the imbalance $\mu_0$ pushes
$H_{00}$ toward zero with $L_0 = 1/4$ unchanged. We instantiate a standardized
binary-logistic design (n=500, p=1000, s=10, $\rho = 0.6$,
$\lambda = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$) and sweep $\mu_0 \in \{0.5, 0.7, 0.9\}$,
comparing the three strategies under cyclic coordinate descent.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-simulated
#| fig-cap: Convergence trajectories for the three intercept strategies on a
#|   standardized binary-logistic design ($n=500$, $p=1000$, $s=10$, $\rho =
#|   0.6$, $\lambda = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$) under cyclic CD, across three
#|   class-imbalance levels. The gradient strategy is competitive only at $\mu_0
#|   = 0.5$ (where $H_{00} \approx L_0$) and falls behind as $\mu_0$ grows,
#|   matching @lem-gradient-partial. The Newton and convergence strategies trace
#|   nearly identical trajectories on all three panels.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-logreg-mu.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals])
df.μ0 = "μₒ = " .* string.(df.μ0)

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-20)

spec = data(df) * mapping(
    :time => "Time (s)",
    :relgaps => "Relative duality gap",
    color = :strategy,
    col = :μ0,
)

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10,),
    facet = (; linkxaxes = :none),
    figure = (; size = (800, 300))
)
```

@fig-simulated confirms the qualitative prediction: at $\mu_0 = 0.5$ the
gradient strategy keeps up, by $\mu_0 = 0.7$ it has visibly slowed, and at
$\mu_0 = 0.9$ it trails the Newton-class strategies by more than an order of
magnitude in pass count to reach a fixed relative gap. The bare-Newton and
convergence trajectories overlay each other throughout, consistent with
@lem-convergence-cost predicting equal per-pass progress and differing only in
inner-step cost---a difference we make visible in @sec-per-pass-cost. The
quantitative scaling of the gradient/Newton ratio with $\mu_0$ and $\lambda$ is
taken up in @sec-imbalance-reg.

### Real Data

The complementary prediction is that the same scaling holds across real problems
with different $(\mu_0,\text{density},n,p)$. We run the three strategies on four
LIBSVM benchmark problems at $\lambda = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$: w1a (n = 2477, p
= 300, sparse, $\mu_0 = 0.029$), leukemia (n = 38, p = 7129, dense,
$\mu_0 = 0.711$), breast-cancer (n = 683, p = 10, dense, $\mu_0 = 0.35$) and
gisette (n = 6000, p = 5000, dense, $\mu_0 = 0.5$). gisette occupies the
$\mu_0 \to 0.5$, $H_{00}/L_0 \to 1$ corner where the gradient strategy is not
predicted to be slow.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-real-logreg
#| fig-cap: Convergence trajectories for the three intercept strategies on four
#|   LIBSVM benchmark problems at $\lambda = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$. The gradient
#|   strategy hits the pass budget on the extremely imbalanced w1a; the
#|   convergence strategy fails to converge on w1a under cyclic CD (see
#|   @sec-ordering). On the well-balanced problems (leukemia, breast-cancer,
#|   gisette) the three strategies are within a small factor of each other.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "real-logreg.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals])

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-20)
df.dataset = replace.(df.dataset, "gisette_scale" => "gisette")

spec = data(df) * mapping(
    :time => "Time (s)",
    :relgaps => "Relative duality gap",
    color = :strategy,
    col = :dataset,
)

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec,
    axis = (yscale = log10,),
    facet = (; linkxaxes = :none),
    figure = (; size = (900, 300))
)
```

@fig-real-logreg confirms the prediction in both directions. w1a is the extreme
imbalance case ($\mu_0 = 0.029$): the gradient strategy fails to reach the
working tolerance within the 1000-pass budget, and the convergence strategy
plateaus around relative gap $10^{-1}$ under cyclic CD---a separate failure mode
that @sec-ordering shows to be specific to coordinate ordering rather than to
the strategy itself. Only bare Newton converges on w1a, and it does so in 232
passes. Leukemia is at the opposite extreme of the regularization-vs-data ratio:
with only 38 samples against 7129 features at $\lambda = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$,
the penalty dominates and all three strategies converge in essentially the same
time. Breast-cancer (n = 683, p = 10, dense) shows the gradient strategy slower
than the Newton-class strategies by roughly a factor of 2.5, milder than w1a as
@lem-gradient-partial predicts for the milder imbalance. gisette is the
predicted benign cell: dense, balanced, $\mu_0 = 0.5$ so $H_{00}/L_0$ is close
to one and the three strategies overlay each other on the convergence panel. The
cross-dataset variation does not isolate a single mechanism the way the
simulated $\mu_0$ sweep does, but it shows the framework's prediction holds at
both ends: gradient is slow when and only when $H_{00}/L_0$ is small.

### Cyclic vs Permuted Ordering {#sec-ordering}

A separate question is whether the convergence strategy's outright failure on
w1a in @fig-first-example is intrinsic to the strategy or to the cyclic
coordinate ordering it is paired with. @lem-convergence-cost is agnostic to
ordering, but its within-pass drift argument relies on the intercept's
environment changing while the pass is in progress; under strict cyclic order,
that drift can compound into a deterministic worst-case pairing in which the
per-pass intercept solve relinearises around an iterate that has already moved.
Permuted CD breaks the deterministic pairing on each pass, and a finite second
moment on the ordering noise is enough for the within-pass drift to average out.
We rerun the @fig-first-example configuration on w1a under both orderings and
the three strategies.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-first-example-ordering
#| fig-cap: Same configuration as @fig-first-example (w1a, $\lambda =
#|   0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$) under cyclic (top) and permuted (bottom) coordinate
#|   ordering. The convergence strategy diverges under cyclic order and recovers
#|   under permuted order, matching the bare Newton trajectory. The gradient
#|   strategy is slow under both orderings, consistent with
#|   @lem-gradient-partial being ordering-agnostic.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "first-example-ordering.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:time, :relgaps, :gaps, :primals])

df.relgaps .= max.(df.relgaps, 1.0e-20)

spec = data(df) * mapping(
    :time => "Time (s)",
    :relgaps => "Relative duality gap",
    color = :strategy,
    row = :ordering,
)

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec,
    axis = (; yscale = log10),
    figure = (; size = (500, 500))
)
```

@fig-first-example-ordering localises the convergence-strategy failure to the
cyclic-order regime. Under permuted CD, the convergence strategy tracks bare
Newton to the working tolerance; under cyclic order, its iterates oscillate and
the relative gap plateaus around $10^{-1}$ within the pass budget. The gradient
strategy is slow under both orderings, as @lem-gradient-partial predicts:
ordering controls within-pass drift, not the per-coordinate Lipschitz mismatch.
The implication for direct CD is that the conservative recommendation---bare
Newton---is also the ordering-robust one; the convergence strategy is a viable
alternative specifically when ordering is randomised or when warm-starting along
a path keeps the within-pass intercept change small (see @sec-warmstart-path).

### Warm-Started Path {#sec-warmstart-path}

The single-$\lambda$ experiments above stress the strategies in their hardest
regime---cold start, large $|\partial_0 F|$ at iterate zero---which is also the
setting in which the theoretical critique of @lem-convergence-cost and the
imbalance collapse of @lem-gradient-partial bite hardest. Production users
rarely solve a single $\lambda$ in isolation; they sweep a grid
$\lambda_1 > \lambda_2 > \dots > \lambda_K$ and warm-start each subproblem from
the previous solution. As anticipated in the steelman paragraph above,
warm-starting begins each subproblem with $|\partial_0 F|$ already small.
@cor-newton-coupling then predicts that the bare Newton step is essentially
exact at the start, so $k_0 \in \{1, 2\}$ in the convergence strategy and the
$k_0 - 1$ per-pass overhead evaporates. The gradient-strategy collapse should
also soften because the iterate is close to optimum and the $H_{00}/L_0$
shrinkage acts on an already-small residual.

We test this by solving an $\ell_1$-logistic path on two problems---a simulated
standardized design ($n = 500$, $p = 1000$, $s = 10$, $\mu_0 = 0.9$,
$\rho = 0.6$) and the w1a benchmark used in @fig-first-example---over a
geometrically spaced grid of $K = 20$ values from $\lambda_{\max}$ down to
$5 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\lambda_{\max}$. Each subproblem is run to relative-gap
tolerance $10^{-8}$ or to a budget of 300 outer passes / 20 wall-seconds,
whichever comes first. We compare the three strategies, each under both warm
start (initialized from the previous-$\lambda$ solution) and cold start
(re-initialized at zero), and under both cyclic and permuted feature ordering.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-warm-start
#| fig-cap: Outer passes per subproblem along a logistic-regression $\lambda$
#|   path (lower is better). Solid lines mark warm-starts from the previous
#|   $\lambda$; dashed lines mark cold starts at zero. Curves capped at 300
#|   indicate the pass budget was hit before the tolerance. Top row uses cyclic
#|   CD, bottom row uses permuted CD; left column is the simulated imbalanced
#|   problem ($\mu_0 = 0.9$) and right column is w1a.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-warmstart-path.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(
    df,
    [
        :reg_grid,
        :passes,
        :times,
        :init_relgap,
        :final_relgap,
        :init_partial0F,
        :nnz_solution,
    ],
)

df.start_kind = ifelse.(df.warm_start, "warm", "cold")
df.ordering = ifelse.(df.randomize, "permuted", "cyclic")

spec_passes =
    data(df) * mapping(
        :reg_grid => "λ / λ_max",
        :passes => "Outer passes",
        color = :strategy,
        linestyle = :start_kind => "Start",
        col = :dataset,
        row = :ordering,
    )

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec_passes,
    axis = (xscale = log10, yscale = log10),
    figure = (; size = (800, 500)),
)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-warm-start-mechanism
#| fig-cap: Magnitude of the intercept partial derivative $|\partial_0 F|$ at
#|   the initial iterate of each subproblem along the same $\lambda$ path. Cold
#|   start (dashed) is independent of $\lambda$ ---the initial iterate is always
#|   zero, so $|\partial_0 F|$ is the marginal class imbalance and the three
#|   strategies coincide on top of each other. Warm start (solid) shrinks
#|   $|\partial_0 F|$ by several orders of magnitude, placing each subproblem in
#|   the regime where @cor-newton-coupling predicts strategy differences to
#|   compress.

spec_partial =
    data(df) * mapping(
        :reg_grid => "λ / λ_max",
        :init_partial0F => "|∂₀F| at initialization",
        color = :strategy,
        linestyle = :start_kind => "Start",
        col = :dataset,
        row = :ordering,
    )

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec_partial,
    axis = (xscale = log10, yscale = log10),
    figure = (; size = (800, 500)),
)
```

The mechanism panel (@fig-warm-start-mechanism) verifies the premise:
warm-starting drives $|\partial_0 F|$ toward zero as $\lambda$ shrinks and the
previous-$\lambda$ solution moves closer to the current optimum. Cold start, by
contrast, sets the initial iterate to zero at every $\lambda$, so
$|\partial_0 F|$ is the marginal class imbalance---roughly $10^2$ on the
simulated problem and $1.2 \times 10^3$ on w1a, identical across strategies.

The pass-count panel (@fig-warm-start) shows the predicted compression with one
caveat. On both problems and both orderings, warm-starting roughly halves the
number of pass-budget-capped subproblems for the Newton and convergence
strategies (e.g., on w1a from $\sim 8$ to $\sim 3$ out of 20) and brings their
curves on top of each other---this is the steelman prediction of
@lem-convergence-cost: with $|\partial_0 F|$ already small, the $k_0 - 1$
per-pass penalty of the convergence strategy evaporates. Warm-starting also
rescues bare Newton from the cold-start cyclic instability that surfaces at very
