small $\lambda$ on w1a, where the cold-start trajectory diverges entirely.

The compression is uneven, however. The gradient strategy is essentially
unaffected by warm-starting on w1a---both cold and warm hit the pass budget on
11 of 20 subproblems, with the curves overlaying. This is @lem-gradient-partial
biting at every subproblem: the imbalance factor $H_{00}/L_0$ remains
microscopic at the warm-start iterate, so even a near-optimal starting point
cannot compensate for the shrinking correction. The simulated problem
($\mu_0 = 0.9$) sits in the milder regime where all three strategies are
competitive cold, and warm-start contributes only a uniform $\sim 5\%$ reduction
in pass count across the board.

The takeaway: warm-starting validates the steelman for Newton-class strategies
(bare Newton and the convergence strategy converge to each other) but does not
extend the gradient strategy's scope. The recommendation of
@lem-convergence-cost---bare Newton in direct CD, convergence strategy at the
prox-Newton/IRLS boundary---stands, with the addendum that the convergence
strategy becomes a defensible alternative to bare Newton whenever a path solve
is in fact used.

### Per-Pass Cost Decomposition {#sec-per-pass-cost}

The pass-count and wall-clock figures above conflate two distinct quantities
that @lem-convergence-cost separates: the *number of outer passes* needed to
reach a tolerance and the *per-pass inner cost* paid at the intercept update.
The lemma's claim is that the convergence strategy pays $k_0 - 1$ extra inner
Newton steps per outer pass with no commensurate rate improvement, where
$k_0 = O(\log\log(1/\varepsilon))$ is the number of inner steps consumed to
drive $|\partial_0 F| < \varepsilon$ at the end of the pass via quadratic Newton
convergence on the 1D intercept subproblem. We instrument the solver to record
$k_0$ for every outer pass and compare the resulting cost trajectories against
the relative-gap trajectories on the imbalanced simulated design of
@fig-simulated ($n = 500$, $p = 1000$, $s = 10$, cyclic CD,
$\lambda / \lambda_{\max} = 0.05$, tolerance $10^{-8}$), sweeping
$\mu_0 \in \{0.5,\,0.9,\,0.99\}$ to vary the cold-start magnitude of
$|\partial_0 F|$.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-per-pass-cost
#| fig-cap: Per-pass inner Newton steps consumed at the intercept update, as a
#|   function of outer-pass index, for the bare-Newton and convergence
#|   strategies across three imbalance levels. The Newton strategy takes exactly
#|   one inner step by construction. The convergence strategy's $k_0$ spikes at
#|   cold start ($k_0 = 6$ on the most imbalanced design) and tapers to one as
#|   the iterate approaches the joint optimum. The area between the two curves
#|   is the cumulative wasted inner work predicted by @lem-convergence-cost.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-per-pass-cost.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])
df = flatten(df, [:pass, :inner_steps, :cum_inner_steps, :relgap_after, :time])
df.μ0_label = "μ₀ = " .* string.(df.μ0)

spec_cost =
    data(df) * mapping(
        :pass => "Outer pass",
        :inner_steps => "Inner Newton steps per pass (k₀)",
        color = :strategy,
        col = :μ0_label,
    )

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec_cost,
    facet = (; linkyaxes = :all),
    figure = (; size = (800, 260)),
)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-per-pass-progress
#| fig-cap: Relative duality gap after each outer pass on the same runs. The two
#|   strategies trace nearly indistinguishable trajectories despite the
#|   convergence strategy paying 19--62 % more inner Newton steps in total
#|   (compare cumulative areas in @fig-per-pass-cost). The extra inner work per
#|   pass therefore buys no measurable per-pass rate improvement, the empirical
#|   content of the "cost-without-rate-improvement" reading of
#|   @lem-convergence-cost.

spec_prog =
    data(df) * mapping(
        :pass => "Outer pass",
        :relgap_after => "Relative duality gap",
        color = :strategy,
        col = :μ0_label,
    )

draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec_prog,
    axis = (yscale = log10,),
    facet = (; linkyaxes = :all),
    figure = (; size = (800, 260)),
)
```

The two figures together make the $k_0 - 1$ overhead claim concrete.
@fig-per-pass-cost shows $k_0$ peaking at the cold-start pass (6, 4, and 4 inner
steps for $\mu_0 = 0.99,\,0.9,\,0.5$ respectively) and decaying to one by the
time the iterate is near the joint optimum. The relative overhead summed across
the run---total inner Newton steps for convergence divided by the Newton
strategy's pass-count baseline---is $1.19\times$ at $\mu_0 = 0.5$, $1.38\times$
at $\mu_0 = 0.9$, and $1.62\times$ at $\mu_0 = 0.99$, scaling monotonically with
the imbalance that drives $|\partial_0 F|$ at cold start. @fig-per-pass-progress
shows that this extra inner work does not translate into faster per-pass
progress: both strategies trace essentially the same relative-gap curve and
finish in comparable pass counts (Newton: 122/122/125; convergence:
112/116/130). The wasted-work claim is therefore quantitatively visible: the gap
between the two curves in @fig-per-pass-cost integrates to strictly positive
inner Newton work for which @fig-per-pass-progress records no return.

The penalty here is modest because quadratic Newton convergence on the 1D
intercept subproblem keeps $k_0 = O(\log\log(1/\varepsilon))$, well below the
inner-loop cap of 20, and most passes need only a single inner step. The regime
where @lem-convergence-cost bites hardest is the cold-start,
large-$|\partial_0 F|$ window of the first few outer passes; the steelman
regimes in @sec-warmstart-path are precisely those where this window is avoided.

### Imbalance and Regularization {#sec-imbalance-reg}

The single-$\lambda$ experiments above test the framework along one axis at a
time. The quantitative prediction of @cor-rate-gap is two-dimensional: the
gradient/Newton pass-count ratio scales with $L_0/H_{00}(\hat\eta)$, and both
$\lambda$ and $\mu_0$ shift $\hat\eta$ and therefore $H_{00}$. We sweep
$\mu_0 \in \{0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 0.95, 0.99\}$ against
$\lambda/\lambda_{\max} \in \{0.5, 0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.02, 0.01\}$ on the
standardized binary-logistic design of @fig-simulated (3 seeds per cell),
running each strategy to a relative-gap tolerance of $10^{-8}$ or a budget of
5000 outer passes. We report pass counts rather than wall-clock to decouple the
per-coordinate Lipschitz-mismatch prediction from BLAS and memory effects.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-mu-reg-gradient
#| fig-cap: Pass-count ratio $T_{\mathrm{gradient}} / T_{\mathrm{Newton}}$
#|   (log~10~ scale) across the $(\mu_0,\,\lambda/\lambda_{\max})$ plane,
#|   averaged over three seeds. Cells where the gradient strategy hits the
#|   5000-pass budget are clipped; the ratio there is a lower bound. Ratio
#|   increases monotonically with $\mu_0$ along every column and with
#|   $1/\lambda$ along every row, matching the qualitative form of
#|   @cor-rate-gap.

dd = JLD2.load(@projectroot("results", "sim-mu-reg-heatmap.jld2"))
df = DataFrame(dd["results"])

agg = combine(
    groupby(df, [:μ0, :reg, :strategy]),
    :passes => mean => :passes,
)

wide = unstack(agg, [:μ0, :reg], :strategy, :passes)
wide.gradient_ratio = wide.gradient ./ wide.newton
wide.convergence_ratio = wide.convergence ./ wide.newton
wide.reg_str = string.(wide.reg)
wide.μ0_str = string.(wide.μ0)

spec_grad =
    data(wide) * mapping(
        :reg_str => sorter("0.5", "0.2", "0.1", "0.05", "0.02", "0.01") => "λ / λ_max",
        :μ0_str => sorter("0.5", "0.7", "0.9", "0.95", "0.99") => "μ₀",
        :gradient_ratio => log10 => "log₁₀(T_grad / T_Newton)",
    )

draw(
    spec_grad * visual(Heatmap),
    figure = (; size = (560, 320)),
)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-mu-reg-convergence
#| fig-cap: Pass-count ratio $T_{\mathrm{convergence}} / T_{\mathrm{Newton}}$
#|   (log~10~ scale) on the same grid as @fig-mu-reg-gradient, on a centered
#|   diverging colormap with $|\log_{10} \mathrm{ratio}| \le 0.1$. The heatmap
#|   is flat at zero (white) across the plane---outer-pass-equivalent
#|   convergence vs Newton, the prediction of @lem-convergence-cost. No
#|   cyclic-CD blow-up of @sec-ordering surfaces on this generic simulated
#|   design---it is dataset-specific to w1a.

spec_conv =
    data(wide) * mapping(
        :reg_str => sorter("0.5", "0.2", "0.1", "0.05", "0.02", "0.01") => "λ / λ_max",
        :μ0_str => sorter("0.5", "0.7", "0.9", "0.95", "0.99") => "μ₀",
        :convergence_ratio => log10 => "log₁₀(T_conv / T_Newton)",
    )

draw(
    spec_conv * visual(Heatmap),
    scales(Color = (; colormap = :RdBu, colorrange = (-0.1, 0.1))),
    figure = (; size = (560, 320)),
)
```

@fig-mu-reg-gradient is monotone in $\mu_0$ across every column: at fixed
$\lambda$, increasing imbalance grows the gradient/Newton pass-count ratio from
roughly one at $\mu_0 = 0.5$ to about ten at $\mu_0 = 0.99$,
$\lambda = 0.01\,\lambda_{\max}$, where the gradient strategy saturates the
5000-pass budget (the ratio there is a lower bound). The cold-start prediction
$L_0 / H_{00} \approx 1 / (4 \mu_0 (1 - \mu_0))$ gives
$\{1.00, 1.19, 2.78, 5.26, 25.25\}$ for the five $\mu_0$ values; the empirical
ratios at $\lambda = 0.05\,\lambda_{\max}$ (the working regime along glmnet's
path) are $\{1.0, 1.1, 1.8, 2.9, 6.6\}$, tracking the predicted scaling at low
imbalance and undershooting it by a factor of two to four at high imbalance. The
undershoot is consistent with the qualitative reading of @cor-rate-gap: the
iterate spends most passes near $\hat\eta$, where the active features pull
$H_{00}$ above its intercept-only proxy $\mu_0(1-\mu_0)$. As $\lambda$ shrinks
more features activate, predictions spread, $H_{00}$ shrinks toward (and beyond)
the intercept-only value, and the ratio grows: at
$\lambda = 0.01\,\lambda_{\max}$ the empirical row is
$\{1.6, 1.7, 4.2, 6.7, \ge 10.2\}$, closer to the cold-start prediction and
clipped at the high-$\mu_0$ end.

@fig-mu-reg-convergence is flat at zero (ratio $\approx 1$) across the plane,
with no cell departing from the unit ratio by more than about 12 %. This is the
outer-pass content of @lem-convergence-cost: the convergence strategy consumes
the same number of outer passes as bare Newton when both converge. The cost of
the convergence strategy is therefore an inner-step overhead, not an outer-pass
overhead---the quantitative form of which is the $k_0 - 1$ wasted-inner-work
claim of @sec-per-pass-cost. The convergence-strategy failure that surfaces on
w1a under cyclic CD (@sec-ordering) does not appear on this simulated design at
any cell; the cyclic-CD pathology requires the specific combination of design
and ordering that w1a exhibits and is not recovered on a generic standardized
imbalanced problem. Together the two heatmaps verify @cor-rate-gap on a 30-cell
grid: the gradient strategy carries a Lipschitz-mismatch penalty whose
pass-count signature scales with $\mu_0$ and $1/\lambda$, and the convergence
strategy does not.

### Production Solvers {#sec-production-solvers}

The strategy-class predictions of the previous sections are tested here against
six production solvers---across both predicted directions---on the shared
imbalanced logistic problem of @fig-irls-comparison ($n = 500$, $p = 1000$,
$s = 10$, nominal $\mu_0 = 0.99$, realized class imbalance $0.878$,
$\lambda = 0.05 \cdot \lambda_{\max}$). For each solver we sweep its convergence
tolerance and record the actual work performed (number of CD passes, outer
iterations, or wall-clock time, depending on what the solver exposes) and the
primal objective at termination. Suboptimality is plotted against work, both on
a logarithmic scale. The reference primal $F^\star$ is taken as the minimum
primal achieved by that solver across all configurations.

The within-package mode comparisons (glmnet, biglasso) isolate the weight-scheme
choice: identical solver, identical problem, identical tolerance, only the IRLS
weighting changes. The third panel runs skglm, the cleanest production
realization of constant-Lipschitz proximal CD, where the intercept update is the
gradient strategy with $L_0 = n/4$ by construction. The fourth panel verifies
the complementary prediction on LIBLINEAR (newGLMNET) and BlitzL1, two
prox-Newton solvers that apply the convergence strategy to the intercept and
that the framework predicts should converge fast. A fifth panel runs adelie
[@yang2024], a recent local-IRLS solver that places the intercept implicitly at
the optimum of each Gaussian surrogate through a weighted-centered-features
parameterization. The framework places adelie in the same bucket as glmnet
`Newton` and biglasso `Newton`, and predicts fast convergence in the working
tolerance regime.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-real-glmnet
#| fig-cap: glmnet `type.logistic = "Newton"` (Bucket B, local-IRLS) versus
#|   `"modified.Newton"` (Bucket A, MM-IRLS with $w \equiv 1/4$) on the shared
#|   imbalanced logistic problem. Both modes converge to the same $F^\star$, but
#|   the MM mode requires roughly six times more inner passes at every tolerance
#|   level---the predicted slowdown from Lemma @lem-gradient-partial applied to
#|   glmnet's `modified.Newton` intercept update.

df = DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "glmnet.csv")))
df.subopt = max.(df.primal .- minimum(df.primal), 1.0e-15)
df.mode = df.type

spec = data(df) * mapping(:npasses, :subopt, color = :mode)
draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec + visual(Scatter) * spec,
    axis = (
        xscale = log10,
        yscale = log10,
        xlabel = "Inner CD passes",
        ylabel = "Primal suboptimality",
    ),
    figure = (; size = (550, 300)),
)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-real-biglasso
#| fig-cap: biglasso `alg.logistic = "Newton"` (Bucket B, local-IRLS) versus
#|   `"MM"` (Bucket A, MM-IRLS) on the same problem. The MM mode requires
#|   roughly ten times more passes than Newton at tight tolerance, an
#|   independent confirmation of the glmnet result on a different codebase.
#|   biglasso documents its MM option as the memory-efficient choice for
#|   out-of-core data; the analysis here quantifies its convergence cost.

df = DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "biglasso.csv")))
df.subopt = max.(df.primal .- minimum(df.primal), 1.0e-15)
df.mode = df.alg

spec = data(df) * mapping(:npasses, :subopt, color = :mode)
draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec + visual(Scatter) * spec,
    axis = (
        xscale = log10,
        yscale = log10,
        xlabel = "Inner CD passes",
        ylabel = "Primal suboptimality",
    ),
    figure = (; size = (550, 300)),
)
```

```{julia}
#| label: fig-real-skglm
#| fig-cap: skglm `AndersonCD` on the same problem. The solver uses constant
#|   per-coordinate Lipschitz steps with the global $1/4$ majorant for the
#|   logistic Hessian and updates the intercept with step $4/n$---exactly the
#|   gradient strategy in our framework. The trajectory exhibits a slow early
#|   ramp (hundreds of outer iterations spent reducing suboptimality from $\sim
#|   0.5$ to $\sim 10^{-5}$) followed by sharp convergence once the intercept
#|   has caught up. The slow ramp is the Lemma @lem-gradient-partial signature;
#|   the post-convergence scatter at high $n_{\text{iter}}$ reflects Anderson
#|   acceleration's non-monotonic stopping behaviour near $F^\star$.

df = DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "skglm.csv")))
df.subopt = max.(df.primal .- minimum(df.primal), 1.0e-15)
df = df[df.n_iter .> 0, :]
sort!(df, :n_iter)

spec = data(df) * mapping(:n_iter, :subopt)
draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec + visual(Scatter) * spec,
    axis = (
        xscale = log10,
        yscale = log10,
        xlabel = "AndersonCD outer iterations",
        ylabel = "Primal suboptimality",
    ),
    figure = (; size = (550, 300)),
)
```

Across the three solvers the prediction holds: within-package weight toggles in
glmnet and biglasso produce the predicted slowdown of the constant-majorant
mode, and skglm---the only production solver in our survey whose intercept
update is unambiguously the gradient strategy---exhibits the slow-ramp signature
that @cor-newton-coupling and @lem-gradient-partial together predict.

The fourth panel verifies the complementary prediction: solvers whose intercept
update is the convergence strategy at a prox-Newton boundary should converge
fast. LIBLINEAR (newGLMNET) and BlitzL1 are the two production solvers in our
survey that fit this description. @fig-real-proxnewton shows both reaching the
optimum within tens of milliseconds of wall-clock time, on the same problem
where skglm needs seconds and glmnet's `modified.Newton` needs roughly an order
of magnitude more inner passes than `Newton`.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-real-proxnewton
#| fig-cap: LIBLINEAR (newGLMNET) and BlitzL1 on the shared imbalanced logistic
#|   problem. Both are prox-Newton solvers that apply the convergence strategy
#|   to the intercept after each linearization, the complement of
#|   `glmnet::Newton` and `biglasso::Newton` from @fig-real-glmnet and
#|   @fig-real-biglasso. Both reach $F^\star$ in tens of milliseconds,
#|   confirming that the convergence-strategy choice on the intercept does not
#|   inherit the imbalance failure mode of the gradient-strategy solvers.
#|   LIBLINEAR runs that hit its internal `max_iter` cap without further
#|   progress have been excluded---they reflect a tolerance-semantic quirk in
#|   the library, not useful work-quality data. Wall-clock time is used as the
#|   work axis because the two solvers count outer iterations differently and
#|   BlitzL1 does not expose an iteration counter on its solution object.

df = DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "proxnewton.csv")))
df.subopt = max.(df.primal .- minimum(df.primal), 1.0e-15)
df = df[.!(df.solver .== "LIBLINEAR" .&& df.n_iter .>= 5000), :]
sort!(df, [:solver, :runtime])

spec = data(df) * mapping(:runtime, :subopt, color = :solver)
draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec + visual(Scatter) * spec,
    axis = (
        xscale = log10,
        yscale = log10,
        xlabel = "Time (s)",
        ylabel = "Primal suboptimality",
    ),
    figure = (; size = (550, 300)),
)
```

The fifth panel adds an independent codebase confirmation for the
convergence-on-the-local-quadratic bucket. adelie\ [@yang2024] is a recent
direct-Newton solver that builds the same weighted Gaussian surrogate as glmnet
`Newton` but realizes the intercept implicitly: rather than updating $\beta_0$
as a coordinate inside the inner CD pass, it weighted-centers the features at
the start of each surrogate and tracks the residual mean, reconstructing
$\beta_0 = \bar{y} + \overline{\mathrm{resid}}$ at the end of the inner solve.
The intercept therefore sits at the surrogate's optimum on every outer pass by
construction, with no separate update step. The classification places adelie in
the same bucket as glmnet `Newton` and biglasso `Newton`, and @fig-real-adelie
confirms the prediction: each tolerance setting completes in tens of
milliseconds in the working range. adelie's outer-IRLS criterion is coarser than
glmnet's coefficient-based `thresh`, which is reflected in a higher achievable
suboptimality from a single tolerance sweep; the per-iteration cost---the
prediction at stake here---is on the same order as the other local-IRLS solvers.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-real-adelie
#| fig-cap: adelie [@yang2024] on the shared imbalanced logistic problem. The
#|   solver is a local-IRLS implementation that keeps the intercept implicit
#|   through a weighted-centered-features parameterization of the Gaussian
#|   surrogate, so on each surrogate the intercept is at the optimum by
#|   construction. The framework places it in the same bucket as glmnet `Newton`
#|   and biglasso `Newton`. In the working tolerance regime each tolerance
#|   setting completes in tens of milliseconds, matching the
#|   convergence-strategy prediction. Tighter tolerances are bounded by adelie's
#|   outer-IRLS criterion $|\sum (\mathrm{resid} -
#|   \mathrm{resid}_{\mathrm{prev}}) \cdot (\eta - \eta_{\mathrm{prev}})| \le
#|   \texttt{irls\_tol}$, which has trouble making progress under imbalance and
#|   effectively places a floor on the achievable suboptimality from a single
#|   tolerance sweep---a property of the criterion, not of the per-iteration
#|   cost.

df = DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "adelie.csv")))
df_ref = DataFrame(CSV.File(@projectroot("results", "real-solvers", "skglm.csv")))
F_star = minimum(df_ref.primal)
df.subopt = max.(df.primal .- F_star, 1.0e-15)
sort!(df, :tol)

spec = data(df) * mapping(:tol, :subopt)
draw(
    visual(Lines) * spec + visual(Scatter) * spec,
    axis = (
        xscale = log10,
        xreversed = true,
        yscale = log10,
        xlabel = "Convergence tolerance (tol = irls_tol)",
        ylabel = "Primal suboptimality",
    ),
    figure = (; size = (550, 300)),
)
```

## Discussion

The picture that emerges across theory and experiments is that the intercept
update is not a one-line implementation detail but a load-bearing choice whose
right setting is dictated by the response distribution. For direct coordinate
descent on a smooth GLM loss, the recommendation is the bare Newton block step:
it is locally invariant to imbalance, requires no tuning, and matches the
convergence strategy on outer-pass count while avoiding the $k_0 - 1$ wasted
inner work that the convergence strategy spends per pass. The damped
(Armijo-safeguarded) variant adds a thin safety net for the narrow cold-start
regime in which a bare Newton step can overshoot\ (@fig-cold-start); in our
experiments the line search succeeds on the first attempt at every iterate away
from cold start, so the damped variant reduces to bare Newton in steady state.
The gradient strategy, by contrast, inherits a per-coordinate Lipschitz mismatch
$H_{00}/L_0$ that shrinks toward zero under imbalance---the same scaling that
produces the order-of-magnitude pass-count gaps in @fig-mu-extreme,
@fig-mu-reg-gradient, and the gradient curve of @fig-multinomial-sweep.

The structural classification of production solvers in @sec-production-solvers
tightens the recommendation into a diagnostic: given a CD-based GLM solver, the
intercept-update strategy it realises predicts whether its inner solve will slow
under imbalance, independent of the rest of the algorithm. The classification
places glmnet `Newton`, biglasso `Newton`, adelie, LIBLINEAR, and BlitzL1 in the
safe bucket and glmnet `modified.Newton`, biglasso `MM`, and skglm in the
imbalance-sensitive bucket, with the predicted pass-count separation confirmed
empirically on a shared imbalanced problem (@fig-real-glmnet--@fig-real-adelie).
The within-package mode toggles in glmnet and biglasso turn this into a
controlled experiment whose outcome is consistent with the framework.

The multinomial setting amplifies the practical relevance of the choice. Whereas
binary logistic regression needs an explicit imbalance ($\mu_0$ near zero or
one) to expose the gradient-strategy stall, the $(K-1)$-block intercept Hessian
distributes the same failure mode across every rare class, so any classification
problem with a long-tailed label distribution sits in the regime where the
gradient strategy is slow on at least one intercept coordinate
(@fig-multinomial-imbalance, @fig-multinomial-sweep). The same multinomial block
structure couples the bare and damped Newton steps with the convergence
strategy, so the scalar wedge between them collapses---a structural property
rather than a tuning artefact, as the 2-D sweep shows.

Two limitations bound the present analysis. First, the Newton-strategy results
are *local*: @lem-newton-approx and @cor-newton-coupling are Taylor identities
for a single Newton step, not a global convergence proof for
CD-with-Newton-intercept, and the empirical evidence in §Results stands in for
that. A tighter rate analysis under restricted strong convexity would let the
corollary of @cor-rate-gap predict the empirical pass-count constant rather than
only its scaling---currently the prediction matches within a factor of two to
four\ (@fig-mu-reg-gradient). Second, the production-solver experiments in
@sec-production-solvers run on a single shared problem; the heatmap of
@sec-imbalance-reg replicates the binary direct-CD predictions across a 30-cell
grid but the cross-package comparison does not yet sweep the $(\mu_0, \lambda)$
plane. Extending the production-solver sweep along those axes, and verifying the
multinomial predictions against glmnet's symmetric-multinomial path and adelie's
multi-response solver, are natural follow-ups.
